CLIPPER SHIP "GREAT REPUBLIC"
The front cover of this menu is a reproduction of an authentic Currier & Ives clipper ship print.
Currier & Ives, known as the "Printmakers of America", graphically preserved the glorious clipper
ship era in a magnificent series of clipper ship prints. This print, one of a series, is being reproduced
through the courtesy of The Mariners Museum, Newport News, Virginia.
The clipper ship "Great Republic" stood for the summit of achievement in the world of sailing
ships. She was, from the standpoint of size, appearance and cost, exactly what her builder Donald
McKay had originally intended to name her: The King of Clippers. The triumph of marine archi-
tecture was launched in 1853 in East Boston. The "Great Republic" was considered the largest,
sharpest and most magnificent craft that was ever produced by any nation of age.
On the night of December 26th, before she had barely tasted salt water, fire broke out on
Front Street in New York and within minutes, the rigging of the "Great Republic", lying at wharf,
was a network of flames. The ship was rebuilt, but her former tonnage of 4,555 tons was reduced
and her sail plan and spars cut down so that she needed only half of her original 130 man crew.
Nevertheless, she served her new owners well and remained the largest merchant ship of her time.
Like Pan Am's modern Clippers* of the air, the early clipper ships traveled the lanes of com-
merce to all the far places of the world... to Japan... to Australia... and, in the days of the
great gold rush, from America's east coast, around Cape Horn, South America, to California.
Our current equipment...the the Clipper fleet of the Twentieth Century... consists of the finest
commercial aircraft ever developed—aircraft that have helped us establish an unparalleled record
for safety, speed and service.
